slides.title: Copilot made beta dispatchers more productive, but volunteers from larger accounts may overstate the gain

claims.claim: 9 pp more jobs scheduled per dispatcher-hour than matched accounts
evidence: Beta accounts rose 11%, matched accounts 2%
The only outcome measured in the product, against each account's prior 12 weeks
240 volunteer accounts over 12 weeks, compared with matched non-beta accounts, 2026

claims.claim: 4.1 dispatcher hours saved a week, self-reported
evidence: No matched comparison exists for this measure
Reported by the dispatchers themselves, not logged by the product
Usage logs in the launch cohort should confirm it

claims.claim: 4 pp higher 90-day renewal than matched accounts
evidence: 97% of beta accounts renewed, against 93% of matched accounts
Volunteers were more active to begin with, so part of the gap is who signed up
Too early to count as lower churn in the business case

claims.claim: Treat the beta results as a ceiling
evidence: volunteers averaged 8.1 seats, against 6.2 for the whole base
the beta ran free of charge, with volunteer accounts only

slides.title: Paying demand is far below the survey: 14% of beta accounts bought Copilot, while 46% of respondents said they would

claims.claim: 3.3x the survey's likely-to-buy share, compared with the share that actually paid
evidence: Survey: likely or very likely to buy: 0.46; Paywall test: bought: 0.14
Survey: October 2026, 610 of 9,800 account admins. Paywall test: last four weeks of the beta, 17 of 120 beta accounts offered Copilot at $149

claims.claim: Survey: only 6% of admins replied, and respondents average 9.4 seats against 6.2 across all accounts
Paywall test: real purchases, but by volunteers who are larger and more active than the base, so even this rate is a ceiling
Who paid: heavy users pick themselves into a paid add-on
evidence: buyers averaged 6,800 requests a month

slides.title: Counting real purchase rates and running costs, the $8M add-on case shrinks to about $0.8M of gross profit a year

claims.claim: Most of the gap is demand that was said, not paid
evidence: CPO case 8; Survey overstatement 5.55; Inference 1.01; Platform 0.6; Gross profit 0.845 ($M)
Survey overstatement: the largest step, from pricing on the survey's stated intent instead of the paywall test

claims.claim: Inference: the accounts that buy are the heaviest users, so the add-on keeps only about 59 cents of each dollar after inference
evidence: 1,372 buying accounts × 6,800 requests a month × $0.009 × 12

claims.claim: Platform: a fixed cost that does not shrink if uptake is low
Add-on ARR at the paywall rate: $2.5M ARR in the first year
evidence: 9,800 customer accounts × 14% bought in the paywall test × $149 per account per month × 12 months = $2.5M

claims.claim: Not yet counted: the one-time $1.47M build cost
evidence: Gross profit before the one-time build cost of 14 engineers for two quarters

slides.title: Routewise's AI coincided with our win rate falling to 37%, but recovering it adds at most $0.6M of ARR a year

claims.claim: AI is now expected in the plan, but the win-back is small
evidence: Win rate in deals where Routewise competed: Q1–Q2 2026 0.44; Q3 2026 0.37
Q3 2026: Routewise put AI in its Pro plan and offered 20% off the first year in the same quarter
Loss notes: 31% mention AI, which shows interest, not cause

claims.claim: Sales' figure: a third of all losses, $1.93M, is three times what the fall is worth
Most the fall is worth, new ARR a year: $0.6M
evidence: 1,560 Routewise deals × 7 pp × $5,878 per new account
new-customer ARR does not count toward net revenue retention

slides.title: Pro beats the $149 add-on on ARR, profit and fit with Routewise, provided it wins twice as many accounts

claims.claim: Half the price for a typical account
evidence: Price a month, 6.2-seat account: $149 add-on vs $74.4 Pro

claims.claim: Pro earns $893 a year per account against $1,788, so it must win twice as many; the Q1 test checks this
evidence: Accounts that take it: 14% add-on vs 33% Pro

claims.claim: Pro ahead while uptake holds
evidence: New ARR: $2.5M vs $2.9M

claims.claim: Both clear the 4 needed at these rates
evidence: NRR added: 4.3 pp vs 5 pp

claims.claim: Allowance caps Pro's inference cost
evidence: Gross profit a year: $0.8M vs $1.6M
Company margin: add-on 76.2%, Pro 76.9%

claims.claim: Pro pays back in under a year
evidence: Payback of the $1.47M build, years: 1.7 vs 0.9

claims.claim: Closes a price gap in new deals
evidence: Fit with Routewise: add-on sold on top of the plan; Pro included in the plan, as Routewise does

slides.title: Pro would add about $2.9M of ARR if a third of accounts move to it, as with the 2023 tier

claims.claim: Pro plan ARR in the first year: $2.9M new ARR, 5.0 percentage points of NRR
evidence: 9,800 customer accounts on Core today × 33% move to Pro within a year × 6.2 seats × $144 Pro premium per seat a year ($12 × 12) = $2.9M

claims.claim: It clears the $2.3M of expansion the 105% NRR target needs, which takes 26% uptake, on four assumptions
evidence: NRR target: from 101% to 105% by 2028, i.e. 4 percentage points of today's $57.6M ARR

slides.title: The heaviest tenth of accounts would cost more to serve than Pro brings in, making a usage allowance essential

claims.claim: 1.8x a top-decile account's inference cost, compared with what an average account pays for Pro
evidence: Inference cost a month: Top-decile account 130.5; Paywall buyer 61.2; Mean beta account 32.4; Median beta account 17.1; Pro price, average account 74.4
Requests a month: top decile 14,500, paywall buyers 6,800, mean 3,600, median 1,900. Pro price = 6.2 seats × $12

claims.claim: Top decile: a flat price lets a few accounts absorb the margin
evidence: these accounts sent 58% of all requests

claims.claim: Paywall buyers: the accounts willing to pay are the heavy users, nearly twice the mean
Median and mean: a typical account costs well under its Pro price, leaving most of it as margin

slides.title: Unlimited Copilot would push company margin below the 75% floor once Pro accounts average about 5,300 requests a month

claims.claim: Company gross margin with Pro at 33% uptake and unlimited Copilot falls below the 75% floor at higher usage
evidence: Today, no Copilot 0.78; Median usage 0.7696; Mean usage 0.7598; Paywall buyers' usage 0.7413; Top-decile usage 0.6969
Margin floor 75.0%

claims.claim: Requests a month per Pro account where margin hits 75%: 5,300
evidence: $1.85M inference room ÷ 3,234 accounts ÷ 12 ÷ $0.009
Margin = 1 − (today's $12.67M cost + $0.6M platform + inference) ÷ ($57.6M + $2.89M Pro ARR)

claims.claim: An allowance and paid top-ups remove the risk
evidence: At full use: margin stays near 77%; top-ups above it at $0.036 a request earn 75%
Pro allowance per seat, requests a month: 333 = 25% of the $12 seat premium ÷ $0.009 per request
An average 6.2-seat account's allowance is 2,065 requests, above the median beta account

claims.claim: Contract: fixed through December 2027; list prices fell 35%, so revisit at renewal

slides.title: Launch in Q2, then mobile, with gates
Mobile reliability drives 4.5 times as much churn as missing AI, which makes the rewrite delay the launch's real cost

claims.claim: 4.5x churn from mobile reliability, compared with churn to rivals' AI
evidence: Main reason given by churned accounts (n = 1,190): Mobile app reliability 0.27; Price 0.22; Missing integrations 0.15; Went out of business / sold 0.14; Switched for AI features 0.06; Other 0.16

claims.claim: Mobile: the churn it drives is worth up to 3.8 percentage points of NRR a year, close to the 4 the target needs
Customers agree: 38% rank a reliable mobile app as their top request, twice the 19% who rank AI scheduling first
Mobile-driven churn, at most $2.2M ARR lost a year, if churners carry average ARR
evidence: $57.6M ARR today × 14% annual logo churn × 27% of churners cite mobile reliability = $2.2M

claims.claim: AI: matters more for winning new deals than for keeping customers
Launching Copilot needs 14 of 60 engineers for two quarters and delays the mobile app rewrite by two quarters

slides.title: Launching Copilot first costs less retention than making it wait, as long as Pro uptake stays above about 25%

claims.claim: Copilot first wins in the base case, but only narrowly
evidence: NRR forgone: Mobile first: Pro waits, 33% uptake 2.51; Copilot first: mobile waits 1.89; Mobile first: Pro waits, 14% uptake 1.06
Each bar = a year's NRR effect × half a year: mobile 3.8 percentage points a year; Pro 5.0 at 33% uptake and 2.1 at 14%

claims.claim: Copilot first: the mobile cost is a ceiling; it assumes the rewrite would stop every mobile-driven churn on day one
Mobile first at 33% uptake: gives up more NRR and leaves Routewise two more quarters as the only plan with AI inside
Mobile first at 14% uptake: cheaper than Copilot first, which is why the Q1 offer test comes before the launch commitment
24.9% Pro uptake where both orders cost the same
evidence: 33% base uptake × 1.9 ÷ 2.5 percentage points of NRR forgone

slides.title: Pro holds margin even at the 14% paywall rate, but would then miss the NRR target and favor mobile first

claims.claim: The input the answer turns on
evidence: Accounts moving to Pro: Base 33%; Stress 14%

claims.claim: Stress falls short of the $2.3M needed
evidence: New ARR: $2.9M vs $1.2M
9,800 customer accounts × 14% move to Pro × $893 Pro revenue per average account a year = $1.2M

claims.claim: Why the Q1 test is a gate / At the stress rate Pro misses the target, and the add-on is the better fallback
evidence: NRR added: 5 pp vs 2.1 pp

claims.claim: Positive in both
evidence: Pro gross profit a year, allowance fully used: $1.6M vs $0.3M

claims.claim: Above 75% in both
evidence: Company gross margin: 76.9% vs 76.9%

claims.claim: Flips below 25% uptake
evidence: Better order: Copilot first (base) vs Mobile first (stress)

claims.claim: Without the allowance, Pro at 33% uptake and paywall buyers' usage of 6,800 requests would lose about $0.09M a year
evidence: All cases include $0.6M of platform cost

slides.title: Four gates let the executive team switch package or order before the cost is sunk

claims.claim: Gate 1: Pro conversion compared with add-on conversion in a randomized two-offer test
evidence: Threshold: Pro wins fewer than twice as many accounts; When: End of March 2027, after one build quarter; If crossed: Launch the $149 add-on in Q2 instead of Pro
2.0x = add-on revenue per account ÷ Pro revenue per account (p. 9)

claims.claim: Gate 2: Win rate against Routewise in Q4 2026, after its promotion ended
evidence: Threshold: Back to 44% or more; When: January 2027 planning; If crossed: Treat the Q3 fall as price-driven; drop win-back from the case

claims.claim: Gate 3: Share of accounts on Pro six months after launch
evidence: Threshold: Below 13%, half the 26% a year the NRR target needs; When: Q4 2027; If crossed: Offer the $149 add-on to Core accounts alongside Pro
26% = Pro uptake for 4 percentage points of NRR (p. 10)

claims.claim: Gate 4: Mobile rewrite back at full staffing
evidence: Threshold: Any slip beyond the two quarters planned; When: Start of Q3 2027; If crossed: Pause new Copilot features until the rewrite is staffed

claims.claim: If the first gate fails, stopping after one quarter caps the sunk build cost at about $0.74M

normalized.recommendation: Launch Dispatch Copilot in Q2 2027 inside a Pro plan at $12 more per seat with a usage allowance (333 requests per seat a month, with paid top-ups), then restart the mobile rewrite; approve the Q2 2027 launch and 14 engineers for Q1–Q2, subject to four decision gates (starting with a Q1 randomized two-offer test where Pro must win twice the add-on's accounts).

alternatives_considered.option: $149 per account per month add-on (CPO's $8M case)
alternatives_considered.treatment: The $8M add-on case shrinks to about $0.8M of gross profit a year; Pro beats it on ARR, profit and fit with Routewise provided Pro wins twice as many accounts. Kept as fallback: launch the $149 add-on in Q2 instead of Pro if Pro wins fewer than twice as many accounts in the Q1 test; at the stress rate the add-on is the better fallback.

alternatives_considered.option: Pro plan at +$12 a seat with Copilot included
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: $2.9M new ARR, 5 pp NRR, $1.6M gross profit, 0.9-year payback at 33% uptake; included in the plan, as Routewise does.

Rejected: would push company margin below the 75% floor once Pro accounts average about 5,300 requests a month; without the allowance Pro at 33% uptake and paywall buyers' usage would lose about $0.09M a year.

alternatives_considered.option: Mobile first: Pro waits two quarters
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected in base case: at 33% uptake gives up 2.5 pp of NRR vs 1.9 for Copilot first and leaves Routewise two more quarters as the only plan with AI inside; but at 14% uptake mobile first is cheaper, and the better order flips below 25% uptake.

alternatives_considered.option: Copilot first: mobile waits two quarters
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: wins in the base case, but only narrowly; mobile cost is a ceiling.

alternatives_considered.option: Offer the $149 add-on to Core accounts alongside Pro
alternatives_considered.treatment: Contingency if share of accounts on Pro six months after launch is below 13%.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data; every number from the briefing pack
Treat the beta results as a ceiling: volunteers averaged 8.1 seats, against 6.2 for the whole base; the beta ran free of charge, with volunteer accounts only
Hours saved are self-reported, not logged by the product; usage logs in the launch cohort should confirm it
Higher 90-day renewal is too early to count as lower churn in the business case
Survey: only 6% of admins replied, and respondents average 9.4 seats against 6.2
Paywall test rate is a ceiling, as buyers were larger and more active volunteers
Loss notes mentioning AI (31%) show interest, not cause; Routewise also offered 20% off the first year in the same quarter
33% of accounts move to Pro within a year, as they did to the 2023 higher tier, which had no AI; the Q1 offer test checks it
Accounts that move have the average 6.2 seats (beta accounts averaged 8.1)
Core keeps its $79 price, so no account pays more unless it chooses Pro
Pro assumes every account uses its full allowance (worst case)
Inference contract fixed through December 2027; list prices fell 35%, so revisit at renewal
Mobile-driven churn estimate assumes churners carry average ARR
Copilot-first mobile cost is a ceiling; it assumes the rewrite would stop every mobile-driven churn on day one
Gross profit is before the one-time $1.47M build cost
Stress case: at the 14% paywall rate Pro misses the NRR target and mobile first becomes the better order
next_steps: Approve the Q2 2027 launch, 14 engineers for Q1–Q2, and Pro at $12 more per seat with a 333-request allowance — CEO and executive team — January 2027

Confirm that allowance metering and top-up billing fit inside the 14-engineer build — Engineering — January 2027
Pull the Q4 2026 win rate against Routewise and track it each quarter — Sales operations — January 2027
Restart the mobile rewrite at full staffing and open the inference contract renewal — CTO and Finance — Q3 2027
normalized.extraction_notes: The deck had no pictures. Charts came through as series data and are transcribed from that. On slide 2, the stray numbers ("1"–"4", "2") and the page references look like section markers and page numbers, so I left them out of the claims. On slide 4, the big numbers (9 pp, 4.1, 4 pp) and their captions were extracted as separate lines; I paired them by order. On slides 6, 10, 15 and 17, the formula pieces (the × and = signs, the numbers and their labels) were also split up, and I put them back together in order. On slide 10, the four assumptions are recorded under assumptions_and_uncertainties.
